title: Punjab's shared devotional ground
hook: the wheat turns gold, and one spring day means different things to the neighbors who keep it

segments.voice: Yesterday, Punjab's shared devotional ground: Lohri, a winter fire, sesame in the flames, a song for Dulla Bhatti. Did you welcome a newcomer? Day one thousand four hundred ten.

Months after the Lohri fire, the fields have changed color. The wheat planted in the cold is standing gold and heavy, and the sickles are coming out. In the villages there's a fair: drums, swings, sugarcane, bangles on a blanket, young men dancing bhangra with their arms up like they're lifting the whole harvest. The day is Vaisakhi. And if you walked through the crowd asking people what the day means to them, you'd hear more than one answer. Today, one spring day that Punjab's neighbors share, each keeping it in its own way.
screen: `THE WHEAT TURNS GOLD.` → `DRUMS, SWINGS, BHANGRA.` → `MORE THAN ONE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Vaisakhi takes its name from the month of Vaishakh, in the spring. Start with the harvest. For farming families in Punjab, it's the moment the year's work pays off. Months of watching the sky, worrying about rain, and now the grain is ready. Thanks comes before the cutting. Then the Hindu year. For Hindus in Punjab, Vaisakhi is also a new year by the solar calendar, the day the sun enters a new sign. So it's a day for new beginnings. Some families go to bathe in a sacred river or a temple tank at dawn. Some visit the temple, offer the first of the grain, and give to those who have less. A new year starts with a clean body, a full granary, and an open hand. And then the neighbor's meaning. For Sikhs, Vaisakhi remembers the day Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa, kept with processions, prayer and service. That meaning belongs to the Sikh tradition, and Sikhs tell it in their own words. A Hindu family and a Sikh family on the same street can both keep Vaisakhi, side by side, each in its own way, neither one borrowing the other's story. And at the fair, all of them hear the same drums. So shared ground doesn't mean everyone believes the same thing. It means the same day, the same fields, the same harvest, and neighbors who know what the day means to each other.
screen: `NAMED FOR THE MONTH OF VAISHAKH` · `THE HARVEST COMES IN` · `A HINDU NEW YEAR BY THE SUN` · `A NEIGHBOR'S DAY, IN THEIR WORDS`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath slow, and look for what ripened. Think back over the past season of your life. What did you plant that has quietly grown: a skill, a friendship, a habit, a patience you didn't have before? Let one thing come to mind. Hold it the way a farmer holds the first sheaf, with thanks and without boasting. If you pray, you can offer that first sheaf to God. The bell holds the time.
Punjab's shared devotional ground. Today, Vaisakhi: a harvest, a Hindu new year by the sun, and for Sikh neighbors, their own remembrance, each kept its own way. Today's word.
